children.text: A crescent-shaped white sand beach stretching about
7 km

along Mayo Bay on the Pacific side of Mati, Davao Oriental. Known as the home of Philippine skimboarding, it's also a sea turtle nesting ground protected by local youths, and its still-undeveloped, quiet shoreline makes it ideal for a relaxed beach getaway.
Dahican Beach lies in Mati, the capital of Davao Oriental province at the southeastern tip of Mindanao. About
10 km
southeast of downtown Mati, a crescent-shaped white sand beach curves for about
7 km

along Mayo Bay, facing the Pacific. Rows of palm trees line the shore behind the beach, and the sand is fine and white as flour. Instead of large resort complexes, simple beach camps and guesthouses are scattered here and there, keeping the old character of a Philippine beach intact.

What made Dahican famous is skimboarding. The Pacific waves rolling into the shallows here are ideal for the sport, and with national competitions held here and national-level athletes emerging from the area, it's earned the nickname "the skimboarding capital of the Philippines." The "Amihan Boys," young men who grew up on this beach, work as skimboarding and surfing instructors and beach lifeguards, and are also well known for rescuing injured or stranded sea turtles and protecting the nesting grounds.

Dahican Beach is also a nesting site where sea turtles come ashore to lay eggs. If you're lucky, you might join a release event, sending hatchlings back to the sea. Around Mati City you'll also find the Mount Hamiguitan Range Wildlife Sanctuary, a UNESCO World Heritage Site designated in
, and Pujada Bay, named to the "Most Beautiful Bays in the World" club — both appealing to nature-loving travelers.
It takes about
4 hours

by bus from Davao, so there aren't many tourists, letting you stroll the long beach at ease even in peak season. It suits anyone who wants to learn skimboarding or surfing, those looking to relax for a few days on a quiet beach, and travelers interested in ecotourism like sea turtle conservation. It's also a good add-on for residents extending a Davao trip by a day or two to see the Pacific.

Beach camps along the shore offer lessons from local instructors. You'll start with the basics — throwing the board into the shallows, running, and jumping on to glide — and even an hour or two is enough to briefly stand on the board.
From around
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon brings bigger Pacific swells, making it a good time for surfing. Beginners should practice on the smaller waves close to shore with an instructor.

When a release event is held to send hatchlings back to the sea during nesting season, travelers can sometimes join in. Timing depends on hatching conditions, so it's best to ask a local beach camp or conservation group in advance.

Walking barefoot along the beach early in the morning or at dusk lets you fully enjoy the white sand, palm trees, and endless waves. Since the beach faces east, the sunrise here is especially beautiful.
Rent a bangka from downtown Mati to visit Pujada Island, Waniban Island, and other spots in Pujada Bay for snorkeling. Unlike the wavy waters of Dahican, the bay stays calm and clear.
From a viewpoint on the coastal road south of downtown Mati, a peninsula in Pujada Bay looks like a sleeping dinosaur. It's Mati's signature photo spot.

The UNESCO World Heritage-listed Mount Hamiguitan Range is famous for its "pygmy forest" of bonsai-like dwarf trees and as a Philippine eagle habitat. Deeper parts of the protected area need a permit, so check the visitor center for information first.

from Cebu. Mati has a small airport too, but it has almost no scheduled passenger routes, so most travelers go via Davao and continue overland.

. Accommodation is spread out along the beach, so it helps to give the exact name of your lodging. Bangkas for island hopping in Pujada Bay are rented by the boat through the Mati coast or your accommodation.
Facing the Pacific directly on the east coast, Dahican's sea changes character sharply with the season. From
March
to
June
, clear days are common and the sea is comparatively calm, making it the best time for swimming, island hopping, and photography. From
November
to
February
, the northeast monsoon (Amihan) brings bigger waves, which is best for surfing and skimboarding, but rain is more frequent and swimming needs more caution.
Davao Oriental sits a bit outside the main typhoon path, but a strong typhoon occasionally crosses eastern Mindanao, so it's worth checking the forecast around
December
. Mati City holds the Sambuokan Festival around
October
each year to mark its cityhood, with street parades and performances. During Holy Week and the
May
holidays, family travelers from the Davao area increase, and beach accommodation fills up quickly.

Beach camps and small resorts offering skimboarding and surfing lessons are scattered along Dahican Beach. The oldest and best-known is Amihan sa Dahican, run by the Amihan Boys, where lessons, board rental, and accommodation are all available in one place. Beach lodging ranges from simple bungalows at about
a night to air-conditioned, pool-equipped resorts at about
. For a wider choice of restaurants and amenities, staying at a hotel in downtown Mati (about
a night) and commuting to the beach is another option.

Fresh seafood and coconut anchor the local food. Grilled Pacific-caught fish and kinilaw, grilled squid, and coconut-milk ginataan dishes are common, and coconut juice fresh from the shell is perfect for quenching thirst after surfing. Davao Oriental is one of the Philippines' major coconut-growing regions, so coconut candy and coconut vinegar also make good souvenirs. There aren't many beach restaurants, so most visitors rely mainly on their accommodation's kitchen, while the downtown Mati market offers cheap fruit and seafood.
There's no ATM around Dahican Beach. Bring enough cash from downtown Mati or Davao to cover accommodation and lesson fees.
The first bus from Davao to Mati leaves before dawn. Taking an early bus leaves you plenty of time for an afternoon lesson.
Skimboarding involves more falling than you'd expect. Wear a rash guard and board shorts, and be careful not to scrape your knees or elbows.
Midday Pacific sun is very strong. Use reef-safe sunscreen, a hat, and sunglasses, and swim in the morning or late afternoon.
Sea turtle release events don't have a fixed schedule. It's best to ask at your accommodation about hatching status as soon as you arrive.
Phone signal reaches most of the beach but is slow. If you need reliable remote work, a hotel in downtown Mati is a more stable choice.
Sunrise photos are best from Dahican, which faces east, and sunset photos from Pujada Bay, which faces west.
Dahican has strong Pacific waves and rip currents (fast currents that pull from shore out to sea). Especially from
November to February
, swim only in the areas local lifeguards or instructors mark as safe.

At the sea turtle nesting grounds, avoid entering near the nests, touching the turtles, using flash photography, or shining bright lights on the beach at night. Harming turtles or their eggs is strictly punishable by law.
Don't leave trash on the beach, and try to cut back on plastic use — local residents do the beach cleanup and conservation work themselves here.

Travel advisories are in effect for some inland mountainous areas of Davao Oriental. Check your home country's latest travel advisory before you go, and stick to the main coastal road and tourist areas.
It's safer to finish the long Davao–Mati journey during daylight hours whenever possible.
Even calm-looking waves can hide a rip current. Regardless of your swimming ability, don't go out alone into open water — follow the guidance of local instructors or lifeguards.
